==Problem==
Shauna takes five tests, each worth a maximum of <imath>100</imath> points. Her scores on the first three tests are <imath>76</imath> , <imath>94</imath> , and <imath>87</imath> . In order to average <imath>81</imath> for all five tests, what is the lowest score she could earn on one of the other two tests?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }48\qquad\textbf{(B) }52\qquad\textbf{(C) }66\qquad\textbf{(D) }70\qquad\textbf{(E) }74</imath>

==Solution 1==
We should notice that we can turn the information we are given into a linear equation and just solve for our set variables. I'll use the variables <imath>x</imath> and <imath>y</imath> for the scores on the last two tests. <cmath>\frac{76+94+87+x+y}{5} = 81,</cmath> <cmath>\frac{257+x+y}{5} = 81.</cmath> We can now cross multiply to get rid of the denominator. <cmath>257+x+y = 405,</cmath> <cmath>x+y = 148.</cmath> Now that we have this equation, we will assign <imath>y</imath> as the lowest score of the two other tests, and so: <cmath>x = 100,</cmath> <cmath>y=48.</cmath> Now we know that the lowest score on the two other tests is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 48}</imath>.

~ aopsav

==Solution 2==
Right now, she scored <imath>76, 94,</imath> and <imath>87</imath> points, for a total of <imath>257</imath> points. She wants her average to be <imath>81</imath> for her <imath>5</imath> tests, so she needs to score <imath>405</imath> points in total. This means she needs to score a total of <imath>405-257= 
148</imath> points in her next <imath>2</imath> tests. Since the maximum score she can get on one of her <imath>2</imath> tests is <imath>100</imath>, the least possible score she can get is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 48}</imath>.

Note: You can verify that <imath>\boxed{48}</imath> is the right answer because it is the lowest answer out of the 5. Since it is possible to get 48, we are guaranteed that that is the right answer.

==Solution 3==
We can compare each of the scores with the average of <imath>81</imath>:
<imath>76</imath> <imath>\rightarrow</imath> <imath>-5</imath>,
<imath>94</imath> <imath>\rightarrow</imath> <imath>+13</imath>,
<imath>87</imath> <imath>\rightarrow</imath> <imath>+6</imath>,
<imath>100</imath> <imath>\rightarrow</imath> <imath>+19</imath>;

So the last one has to be <imath>-33</imath> (since all the differences have to sum to <imath>0</imath>), which corresponds to <imath>81-33 = \boxed{48}</imath>.

==Solution 4==
We know that she scored <imath>76, 94,</imath> and <imath>87</imath> points on her first <imath>3</imath> tests for a total of <imath>257</imath> points and that she wants her average to be <imath>81</imath> for her <imath>5</imath> total tests. Therefore, she needs to score a total of <imath>405</imath> points. In addition, one of the final <imath>2</imath> tests needs to be the maximum of <imath>100</imath> points, to make the final test score—the one that we are looking for—the lowest score possible for her to earn. We can now see here that the sum of <imath>76+94+100</imath> has a units digit of <imath>0</imath> and that the final test score must have a units digit ending with a <imath>5</imath>. Now, <imath>87</imath> needs to be added to a number that makes the sum divisible by <imath>5</imath>. Among the answer choices of <imath>48, 52, 66, 70,</imath> and <imath>74</imath>, only <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 48}</imath> has a units digit that works. (<imath>48+87=135</imath>, giving us a units digit of <imath>5</imath>.)

~ saxstreak
== Solution 5 (most intuitive) ==
For Shauna to get an average of <imath>81</imath>, she needs to score a total of <imath>81 \times 5 = 405</imath>. One of the final two tests must earn a score of <imath>100</imath> to ensure the final test score is the lowest possible. <imath>76+94+87+100 = 357</imath>, and <imath>405-357 = \boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 48}</imath>.
~themathkidwoohooooo

== Solution 6 (rocket speed) ==
81 times 5 = 405. Adding the units digits of 76, 94, 87, and 100 gives 7. To end with five the fifth score ends with 8 so the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A)}\ 48}</imath>. 

~Supernova77
